utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the court today. Mr. Registrar, may you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel and everyone in and around the Court room. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis and Laurie Sartorio, assisted today by our intern, Ms. Emma Berry, and our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning to my learned friends from the Prosecution and to all those in and around the courtroom. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and I appear here on behalf of Mr. Delic, together with Mr. Robson, with our assistants, Lejla Gluhic and Asja Zujo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis. Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. My name is Jovan Divjak.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what is the date and place of your birth?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: I was born on the 11th of March, 1937, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And where do you currently reside?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Currently, as well as for the last 40 years, I have resided in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not manage to catch the street name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was the street name where you stay in Sarajevo, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I live in Sarajevo, and I've been living there for 41 years in Logavina Street, number 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: I am retired. I was retired in 1997. Currently, I am the executive director of the association named "Education Builds B and H," which as of 1994 has been helping children who were victims of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to please briefly describe for the Chamber your military education/training and the positions that you held in the army.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Having in mind that my mother could not finance the studies I wanted to undertake, in 1956, I went to study at the military academy of the land forces in Belgrade. I completed it in 1959, and I've remained with a unit which was a part of the JNA Guards. For a while in Belgrade, I commanded a platoon. Then I was sent to the School of Foreign Languages that existed within the JNA. In 1962 and 1963, I completed the course in that school. In the meantime, I was with the Tito's Guards. In 1964, in November, I believe, until July 1965, I attended the Command and Staff Academy in Paris, the academy of the French Armed Forces. As of September 1965 until the 1st of February, 1966, I was in Belgrade at the Security Administration. As of February 1966, I performed various duties in Sarajevo in the Centre of Military Schools. For a while, I was a cadet platoon commander; then I commanded a cadet company. And between 1969 and 1971, I completed the Command and Staff Academy. Upon my return to Sarajevo, I commanded the Cadet Battalion there for three years. Later, I was a lecturer at the Tactics Department between 1979 and 1981, 1982. Between 1982 and 1984, I was chief or head of the Tactics Department. As of October 1984, until October 1989, I commanded the Territorial Defence of the Mostar District. From October 1989 until the 1st of October, 1991, I was command of the TO of the District of Sarajevo. Towards the end of September, I was removed from that duty of the commander of the TO of the District of Sarajevo, and I was summoned to appear before a military court, since as the district TO commander, I ordered that a part of the equipment, ammunition, and weapons of the TO in Kiseljak municipality be handed over to the police force of that town, the reason being that at the time the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina had decided that combat readiness be raised to a higher level due to the war that was ongoing in Croatia. The police force of that town was poorly equipped before that. The then commander of the TO in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Drago Vukasjevic, initiated the court proceedings. I was sentenced to two -- nine months in prison and two years probation. At the beginning of the war, or rather, the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the 8th of April, 1992, I was summoned to the Territorial Defence Staff, Bosnia-Herzegovina, where I was offered to become the TO deputy commander for Bosnia-Herzegovina. I remained at that position until the end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a moment, just for clarification, please. Does this mean you did not serve the full nine months' jail sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So when you were called, were you called out from prison? In April 1992, were you called from prison to come and head the Territorial Defence Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was in Sarajevo in the period between the handing down of the sentence in December -- of the judgement in December 1992 until the 8th of April -- I apologise, December 1991, and until the 8th of April. I was on duty at the Republican Staff of the Territorial Defence. Therefore, in the meantime, there was no order for me to go to the prison to serve the sentence. This prison was -- for the officers of the JNA was located in Nis, in Serbia. On the 8th, I was called by Mr. Stjepan Siber, and he told me that these were historic moments for Bosnia-Herzegovina. The cursor doesn't seem to be moving. Should I continue? These were intense moments for Bosnia-Herzegovina, since at that time, the multinational defence was being organised for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I was asked to join the staff. As envisaged, the commander of the staff was supposed to be Colonel Hasan Efendic, and I accepted to be his deputy -- or rather, Mr. Siber told me that he had accepted to be his deputy, and, "We wanted you to be the third person in charge, and please give it a thought and then let us know what you decided." I remained at the staff during the afternoon --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this 1992 you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes, the 8th of April, 1992. I am explaining the events as they occurred in the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina Staff at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. So from April of 1992, what was -- after April 1992, what was your next position that you held?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: As of April 1992, until the end of 1994, I was deputy commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And after 1994, until the 1st of March, 1997, I was assistant commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina for cooperation with civilian structures.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And are you retired now, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: I retired on the 1st of March, 1997, and I am quite content in that situation, I may say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what was your rank at the time you retired?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: I was a brigadier general.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, General, in 1993, did you hold another post? Were you appointed to another post?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: No. There was some separate tasks; however, my duty remained that of deputy commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina throughout.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. But at some point did the -- did the command structure of the army become reorganised?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: For the initial fortnight, what there was the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which in May or June was transformed and renamed into the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As it developed, it saw occasional changes in structure and the way it was organised, starting with the Supreme Command Staff level as well as at the level of the subordinate staffs and commands. We first began with detachments in units. In June and July, we saw the formation of the first brigades; and between September and December of 1992, five corps were formed, and somewhat later the sixth one came into existence. In response to your question, in 1993, there were certain changes in the formation and the establishment of the army, as well as within the staff of the Supreme Command. By way of illustration, I can tell you that the staff, with all of its attached organs, including communications, logistics, et cetera, should comprise over 1.000 people, but its manning strength was never more than 60 per cent of that. Throughout that time until 1994, I was deputy commander, and later on I was appointed assistant.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. In 1993, did you become deputy to General Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Yes, following a decision of the Presidency. On that occasion, it was confirmed that Mr. Siber and Divjak were deputy commanders. It was then for the first time that the function of the command -- of the commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was established in full.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to you briefly tell the Judges, describe for the Judges the organisation of the Presidency in civilian time, how many members and what the election process was.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: The Presidency, before the war, was supposed to be elected, and it comprised seven members; however, the Constitution envisages that in times of war, it can be expanded. The seven Presidency members represented the constituent peoples, meaning that Bosniaks had two representatives, Serbs had two, Croatians two, and the seventh I presumed was from among the other existing peoples in the territory. And during that time, it was Mr. Ganic who at that time declared himself as Yugoslav; therefore, he was not a Bosniak. That was the situation before April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Just a question. Are the seventh -- are the seven members elected by the population?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Yes. There were elections and they gained the most votes, and such representatives were made members of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And was there a president of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: According to the Constitution, the president of the Presidency was elected as the other members, but within the framework of the Presidency. Throughout the war and until after the Dayton Accords, it was Mr. Izetbegovic. He was the president of the Presidency, but he had the same powers as all of the other members of the Presidency did.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Was there -- was the president elected by the members of the Presidency or by the population as a whole?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: The members of the Presidency elected him, or rather, the Parliament. But according to the number of votes, they gained elections. The person who gained the most votes was elected.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And how long -- what was the tenure of this position?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: According to the Constitution and as far as I know, although I'm not fully versed in that, I believe the tenure was four years, with a possibility of extension.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, by the time that you became the -- okay, sorry. Excuse me, I'll ask another question. You said that the Presidency during wartime was expanded and included other departments within the government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: According to the Constitution, there was also supposed to be the commander of the Army of BiH, the president of the Assembly, the Prime Minister, and I'm not sure about the Minister of the Interior, but these were the people. In case of need, when certain subjects were being discussed about Bosnia-Herzegovina, upon the decision of the Presidency, other members may have been included as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And during wartime, what entity or what persons constituted the command, the Supreme Command of the Army?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: The Supreme Command of the Army was the Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina: This was Delic, his deputies, the staff members and everyone else, if we are talking about the army Supreme Command. However, if we are talking about the commander of the armed forces, who was superior to the both the army and the police, then in that case it is the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask, does the Constitution of the Supreme Command change in time of peace? And I'm asking you that question because the question put to you said: "during wartime, what entity or what persons constituted the command, the Supreme Command of the army?" Now, does the Supreme Command of the army change in Constitution during peacetime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Presidency comprised only seven members, as envisaged by the Constitution. However, on the day the war was declared in Bosnia and Herzegovina in June 1992, then the wartime Presidency also comprised the people I mentioned: The Assembly president, the Prime Minister, the commander, and I believe the Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you to be saying that the Presidency and the Supreme Command are one and the same thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As wartime, yes, the Supreme Command is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, General Divjak, by what date would you -- was the organisational structure of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina functioning and operating, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Well, opinions vary; but, in my view, it was on the 8th or the 9th of April, 1992, when the TO Staff for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was founded.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And -- I'm sorry. Excuse me. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: And when we conveyed the Presidency's decision to our subordinate staffs on the organisation of the new staff, and when we advised them that there was a process of reorganisation in the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we forwarded that information to the various Territorial Defences, whereby it was accepted by 73 municipal TO staffs in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So, in 1992 and the first half of 1993, the army was carrying out operations?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: The word "operation" is a strategic term. The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not have the materiel or personnel resources to carry out operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, sir. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was a particularly leading question. I would kindly ask the Prosecutor to be more careful when putting her questions, but the witness had already answered. First of all, she should have established whether it was operational in terms of function and then perhaps go on to any potential operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll withdraw the question and move on, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, prior to June of 1993, could you tell us what your duties were on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Prior to June 1993, as the deputy commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I took part in the planning, organising, and execution of combat operations, first of all, of the Territorial Defence and then of the army, indirectly, of course. I participated in the preparation and drawing up of establishment plans, the organisational structure of the army, and I directly participated in the organisation of the defence by units in Sarajevo initially, and later also outside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you attend meetings?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Well, within the framework of the staff, we had a system that we had introduced, given our experiences in the work of the Territorial Defence in the previous period; namely, we had routine morning briefings to the Administration in the centre. Once a month, we would hold analysis meetings of the realisation of our work plans, that is. We monitored the execution of combat operations, and we had brief analyses of the combat operations, also communicated occasionally to members of the Presidency. The basic problem that we encountered and that we had to cope with, and which we conveyed to the Presidency, was the problem of the materiel support of the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, when you say "we," "We had a system and we met at routine morning briefings," could you please tell us who "we" consist of? Not names, but positions.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: I'm talking about the staff of the Supreme Command of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which in addition to the commander, who occasionally was present, Mr. Halilovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Karlovic"] at the time, also his deputies, that is Mr. Siber, and the heads of administrations or their desk officers. There were eight administrations. And depending on the situation that we were faced with, we would have some of them present to analyse the situation and analyse the reports that were coming in from the subordinated staffs. According mainly to our orders, subordinated staffs had to send us daily reports on what was happening in the zone of responsibility of the corps. So the head of the Security Administration was there; the Intelligence Administration head; the head of the Logistics; Personnel Administration; the Moral Guidance Administration; and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a matter for the record, I noted at page 30, line 5, it states "Mr. Karlovic." The witness stated the commander at that time was Mr. Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Robson. I was also wondering what Karlovic wanted. Thank you. You may proceed, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, sir, who is Mr. Karlovic? What position did he hold?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It should read Halilovic. It is not corrected yet, that is why I was wondering if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's at line 19 to 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I see 13.5 as well. It's fine. I just wanted clarification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, what were matters -- what types of matters were discussed at these meetings? Things that were going on in the field, were those matters discussed?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: That was a routine system. The first item on the agenda was always getting acquainted by the intelligence head of Administration about the combat operations of the aggressor. He conveyed to us later the information that he had received from subordinated staffs; then the operations organ would analyse what the units of the various corps had undertaken and realised, and then the security organ would present their analyses and assessments, and the logistics organs as well. And they would draw their information from the daily reports they received or the information they received directly from their subordinated organs; namely, in addition to the general report which was received from the corps, the Intelligence Administration organ also had its own command-and-control line via which it received information on what was going on. So we received daily information coming from the subordinated units.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: During these meetings, was there ever a discussion involving perhaps disciplinary issues involving troops or soldiers and other types of misbehaviour?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, in June of 1993 -- oh, excuse me. One other question: Did President Izetbegovic attend these meetings on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: No. At that time, and we are talking about 1992 and 1993, there was no need for him to attend these analysis meetings at the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And why was --

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: However, however, I have said that we met at least once a month, the commander, the deputy. Sometimes it would be I, myself. Sometimes it would be Siber. Sometimes Halilovic, as the commander, would actually report, communicate basic data to President Izetbegovic, as the president of the Presidency, and occasionally also to the other members of the Presidency, on the most important issues of the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You wanted to ask me I expect why he wasn't present, because he did not attend because he did not need to and it was not his obligation to attend.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. And you did say that issues were communicated to him as needed; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, when General Delic became the supreme commander of the army, you were one of his two deputies with General Siber; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And General Siber is of Croatian ethnic origin; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Yes. That is how he -- what he declared to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And what is your ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: I am Bosnian; although, this is not recognised under the Constitution. The Constitution of the Federation says that this is a community of Croats, Bosniaks, and others, so it does allow me to be a Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: But you were born in Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Yes. I was born in Belgrade, but that doesn't make me necessarily a Bosnian or a Serbian or an American. I was born there, but my father was a teacher at the time. He hails from Bosnia, the Bosnian Krajina. And the fact that my mother gave birth in a Belgrade hospital doesn't mean anything. I am a Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I understand that, sir, and I respect that. I guess what I'm getting at is: Was there a reason, was there an intentional placement of certain persons in their positions within the Presidency based on their ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Well, under the Bosnia-Herzegovina Constitution, that is a state of three constituent peoples, the Serbs, Croats and Bosniaks, or vice versa, so that the government structure also follows that principle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, when you became the deputy to General Delic, what were your regular duties?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: When Siber and I, myself, were appointed Commander Delic's deputies, it was just a routine assignment. There was nothing knew. What was knew is that the position of the commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was introduced for the first time, and the chief of staff as well, to which post was appointed Sefer Halilovic. So Siber and I, myself, were just a continuation of the positions; actually, we continued to hold the post that we held in the first year of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you attend daily meetings?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Yes. As part of the Operations Centre, we continued to hold regular meetings. We would meet once a month in the presence of Commander Delic in order to undertake monthly analyses of our work and to ascertain the focus of our tasks, our priority tasks for the forthcoming period. General Delic fully trusted us and asked us to brief us about what had transpired, what had been talked about at all those meetings which he personally did not attend. So, in the long run, there was nothing knew. We changed nothing in the system of monitoring events on the ground in the war theatre in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, during these meetings, and your new position, were you ever present when brigade commanders reported?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question is a leading one. I'd ask the prosecuting counsel rephrase her approach. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't believe it's leading. A leading question would be: "You were not present when brigade commanders reported, were you?" That is a leading question. The question is: "Were you?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I expect the objection is to the fact that you're suggesting that brigade commanders did report.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. I'll set the foundation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, what went on at these -- let me just back up. Were these morning -- were these daily meetings?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Yes. In principle, they were morning briefings, but there were also other times when such meetings were held, especially when the monthly analyses were being undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And were the same types of subjects discussed at these morning briefings as were discussed in 1992 and early 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: In 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995, as long as the war lasted, there was a system in place for the morning analyses of what we received from the units. Monthly analyses are another thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to go back to the daily meetings. When were the meetings -- were there meetings where brigade commanders would be reporting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's what was objected against earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I asked were there meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you're suggesting that brigade commanders were making reports. Sir, you've just referred to receiving information from the units. Who gave you the reports from the units? Who presented these reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such information came to us in written form by way of signals, communications equipment, depending on the situation, but it was in writing. That information came to the organs of the staff. So the intelligence organ, for instance, from the 1st or the 3rd Corps directly liaised, communicated, with the operations organ in the Supreme Command Staff; and with that information, the representative of the administration or the head of the Security or Intelligence Administration would come to the morning briefings. At such morning briefings, the commanders of the brigades were not present. They did not attend. I'm talking about the internal mechanism of our work within the staff. There were other different meetings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just follow-up? I just want a very short answer. You said that the information came to you in written form by way of signals. Who wrote this information? Who had signed at the bottom as the author of this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we talk about overall information from the 1st Corps, it would be signed by the commander or his deputy. But if we are talking about information reports coming from a specific service, for instance, I referred to the intelligence service, again, the head of the intelligence service from the 1st Corps would send the report to the head of the Intelligence Administration, and he would sign it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Madam Sartorio, you realise that earlier, at page 19, line 11, the witness does say that commanders of brigades did not attend.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Who was present at these meetings, General Divjak?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: I should like to ask you to make a distinction between what I said were morning reporting sessions, morning briefings, and those which took place during the month, or those things which took place in Sarajevo or outside Sarajevo during the month. At these morning briefings, we had officers from the administrations attending, as I said: The Intelligence Administration, the Security Administration, the Morale Guidance Administration, the Personnel Administration, and others. There, reports would be put together which we had to consolidate in order to propose to the commander what moves to make, what steps to take. When the commander was present at these morning briefings --

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: You may finish now, since it's behind. So go ahead and finish your answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: So on those days when the commander also attended, and Mr. Delic, that is, he would conclude himself what he has to do. That he did on the basis of our analyses and our proposals. He concluded what each of the specific administrations should do, what the Intelligence Administration should do, what information it should elicit from the units. And he ordered the Logistics Administration head how to handle different problems; for instance, to address the problem of the lack of fuel for the 1st Corps. That is the communication that went on at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Was there meetings that you attended where you discussed operation and combat activities?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Unfortunately, at the level of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, no. At the level of the staff, without the presence of the commanders of the subordinate units, we undertook such analyses and proposed the specific solutions to the commander as to how to use the corps units, later divisions. However, when we speak, for instance, about one specific event that I remember vividly, when we were planning how to lift the blockade of Sarajevo in 1995, I was not involved - I don't know why - not to mention some other activities and combat activities outside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you feel that your duties changed in any way before -- after June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: No. I cannot claim that anything changed much after June, anything specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you attend Presidency meetings?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Can I please first finish my previous answer, if it is all right with Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is all right. You may finish. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So even up to June 1993, I had not been fully satisfied. I was not content with the way I was involved in something which was my profession. In fact, I wrote about it to Commander Halilovic, asking him to avail himself of my services more, and I did so on two occasions. On two occasions, actually, I also wrote to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to Mr. Izetbegovic, on the 9th of May, 1992, and on the 27th of May, 1993, requesting that I be used more. So when you say from June 1993, nothing specific actually changed. You asked me whether I participated at Presidency meetings, sessions. Yes, I did. Every time when Commander Delic was officially absent, absent on official business, and when he empowered me to deputize for him in his absence and to attend the Presidency sessions in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Did you ever meet with -- strike that. Do you know of any other meetings that were held with General Delic and other members of the Presidency at which you did not attend?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: I apologise. It was not mine to follow, whether General Delic had any other meetings, special meetings. But what was not clear to me was why, except for two times, except for on two occasions, I did not attend the reports by corps commanders which were being carried out, for the most part, outside Sarajevo. Sometimes, in order to actually calm myself, I would think to myself this was probably because it was very difficult to get outside this occupied city of Sarajevo. But I would like to repeat, on this occasion as well, I regret the fact that in the planning of combat operations, when this was being done by the commander with his assistants and other heads, that I never had the occasion to state my mind and to say what I thought could have been of help. I should like to convey here an assessment of General Delic's. I know that this is what he thought, and that was that Divjak was one of the best-schooled officers in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, as deputy commander to General Delic, were you involved in any decision-making with regard to military operational matters?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: I apologise to you, but I believe that it is quite clear. It follows from my previous answer, that I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Were you ever consulted by General Delic on any matters with regard to military operational matters?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Having assumed the position of commander, General Delic wanted to regulate the relations in the staff, seeking for them to be more functional than previously; therefore, he assigned to me the task, and to General Siber who at the time was a colonel. So he gave us a task to write up the assignments which would have to be carried out by deputies. Siber and I were not completely happy with the fact that Commander Delic only very infrequently asked us for our opinions. I believe that, in fact, General Siber was much more in a position to talk about problems related to the organising of the armed struggle. I do not recall him having ever consulted me in connection with the execution of combat operations, and I can say that the -- that General Delic's idea was that I was to be -- it was his idea that I should be assistant for cooperation with civilian structures. He probably thought me capable of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you ever involved in any discussions or decision-making matters regarding the formation of corps, brigades, units, or other formations? I'm talking about after June of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: These are technical issues, and we were involved in those; the composition of the corps, the composition of the units, armaments, weapons. There were no problems there, because this process was carried out by the personnel and mobilisation administrations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Were you involved in the discussions regarding the formation of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: No, not directly, but indirectly I will tell you presently: In July 1992, when the setting up of brigades began, it was pointed out that some of those brigades should be designated Muslim brigades. I stated my opinion that that would not be all right, given the fact that this was the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the army of all defenders, not only Bosniaks and Muslims. There had even been ideas to suggest that Serbian brigades should be set up, including in Sarajevo, and I was against that, too. I insisted that really the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina can be conducted by all its citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now, at some point, and I'd like to concentrate now on the time period from June 1993 to the end of the war, did you feel that the ethnic composition of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was changing in any way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, I object to that. It's a leading question. Obviously, the Prosecution can ask about the ethnic composition at certain periods of time, but this clearly seeking a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I disagree, Your Honour. That's one of the purposes why the witness is here, to talk about certain things that he wishes to tell the Chamber. If you want me to ask ten questions to get to where -- to this point, I'll do that. But I don't believe it's a leading question. A leading question would be: "Isn't it true that the ethnic composition changed?" I didn't ask that question. I asked him what his belief was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want his belief or do you want fact?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Both. He can -- he can state his belief, and then he can state upon what his belief is based, if he can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I suppose a question formulated somewhat like: "Did the ethnic composition of the army change at any stage," would be a fair question. But when you say "do you feel," "did you feel," I'm not quite sure whether his feelings here are very apposite here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll take that suggestion and ask the question -- rephrase the question, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: General Divjak, given your position in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and your participation in the Supreme Command Presidency, did the ethnic composition of the army changed after June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: It began changing after some five or six months of existence of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Whether someone intended for those changes to occur, I don't know. What I can say is that for a certain while the staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in a way was a structure corresponding to the situation in the field. Let me be clear. I do not mean the ethnic makeup as it existed in 1991. When we talk about the various elements, for example, the soldiers in the army who were of Serb origin, then I have in mind those who remained in the territory where the majority of the population were Bosniaks. Please bear that in mind. You should also know that many Sarajevo citizens of Serbian and Croatian origin kept telling me and Siber that they remained there because of us, for we represented, we embodied that idea of the multi-ethnic armed force. Percentages vary, whether there were 12 per cent of Serbs and 18 per cent of Croats in the staff of the Army of B and H. However, the fact is that until the end of 1993 and early 1994, in high-ranking positions, there were both Croats and Serbs, or rather, there were there up until that time, and there were not after that. There were several explanations for that which I cannot accept. Some tried to explain that a certain number of Croats and Serbs fled to the other side because they were distrustful of the division envisaged by Vance and Owen. They were uncertain of their fate if they remained in the federation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you did not accept that explanation?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: I cannot accept that for a simple reason, this being that among the soldiers who had deserted from the army, in overall percentage, there were more soldiers of other nationalities and more Bosniaks than Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, were you involved or do you have knowledge of training of soldiers in Sarajevo in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Based on the warfare conducted by the partisans, and knowing that it is necessary for any army to have training in place, Sefer Halilovic, on my suggestion, organised training of soldiers and detachment leaders, as well as commanders of the platoons, companies, and up to the level of battalion. The similar thing was done in other corps as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can you tell the Chamber what the ethnic composition was of the training -- the population of soldiers who were trained?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Reflecting the number of Orthodox and Catholic soldiers in the units, that is, Serbs and Croats, I wished that that number had been greater. I can tell you that in April 1993, at the end of the one-year-long training at the Centre for Training in Sarajevo at Bjelave, out of 2.400 soldiers who completed different command courses, among those there were only 15 Serbs and 20 Croats, or the other way around, but that was it. They were the only ones of any other nationality. I advised Commander Halilovic of that. I even sent a letter to the Sarajevo Corps that would stress the fact that attention had to be paid, that a greater number of soldiers of other nationalities, other than Bosniaks, should attend such command courses.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know about the Higher Command or Officers' School? Are you familiar with that entity?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: When the forming of the school took place in Zenica, I had no role there. I did, however, appear there twice to lecture. However, in 1995, I participated in the Division command training, and I have positive impressions of that course. The commanders there told me that I was one of the most and best qualified teachers they saw at that brigade commanders course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. From 1993 to 1995, do you know the ethnic composition of those soldiers, those potential commanders who attended?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: I can only tell you about the Division commanders course. As far as I can see, it was a uni-ethnic composition of soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And, please, just what do you mean by "uni-ethnic composition," sir?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: I mean to say that there were only Bosniaks attending the course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And by "Bosniaks," do you mean Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Until August 1993, they were referred to as "Muslims." However, at an intellectual gathering that day, they established that the term "Muslim" is obsolete and that for a hundred years the term "Bosniak" was banned. And they reinstated that term, the term "Bosniak," which was then also included in the Dayton Constitution. The term "Bosniak," however, is not accepted by the other two ethnic groups, that is, Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: All right. And one last question before the break: Do you know, approximately, how many attendees there were at this commanders school during 1993-1995?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: What happened in Zenica at the wartime commanders staff school, I don't know; but at the brigade commanders course, there were 26 or 27.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And you don't recall the number for the other schools?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: I had nothing to do with the other schools. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That's a good time to take a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Given the fact that we started late this morning and we have sort of been thrown out of kilter, our schedule has been thrown out of kilter, we suggest going until 12.00, and then we can back to our normal time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: That's fine. I am going to try to finish today Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I am sorry. I thought you said we would break until 12.00, and then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sorry. What I said was I thought you told me we would take a break until 12.00 and then come back. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: We just talked about the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. Do you know who was involved in the formation of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: I believe the people who had been thrown out of their homes. The word is "Mujahedin" [as interpreted]. Those were the people who were expelled from the Drina Valley and elsewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Not "Mujahedin," "Mujahid"" [as interpreted], not the "Mujahedin."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'm asking you if you know who was involved in the formation of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: I told you who comprised the brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic. Can we just correct that?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the transcript, perhaps the witness could spell out the word he uttered. He said "Mujahid." The two words "Mujahedin" and "Mujahid" are similar, but perhaps the witness can spell it out for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could the witness spell the word he pronounced.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] M-U-D-Z-A-H-D-E, if I'm correct. Perhaps I'm wrong. "Mudzahde" or "Muhajid," I don't know. Help me, please. Help me out. "Mudzahir."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please, can we stop typing this "Mujahid." We are trying to get the correct name. Now, if you keep typing this "Mujahid" next to "Mudzahde," you're causing the confusion even further. It's M-U-D-Z-A-H-D-E; that's what we want.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] M-U-D-Z-A-H-I-R. I think this is it: "Mudzahir."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: M-U-D-Z-A-H-I-R. Okay. "Mudzahir." Okay. Thank you very much. You may proceed now, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know when this unit was formed?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: I think in early 1993. I'm not sure, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And do you know who was involved in the formation of this unit?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: It was formed at the level of the corps, the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And do you know what the purpose was of this unit?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: According to the explanation given, and after the discussion we had at the staff, it was concluded that it was supposed to be an elite unit, to be used at such positions or locations at the front line that were in danger, that were under the most pressure by the opposing party. For me, it also meant that they could provide moral support to the Bosniak people in their defence against the aggressor. I said that these people were refugees. They had been expelled from their century-long homes, and their ultimate goal to all of them was to return to the places they hailed from.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Are you aware of any disciplinary problems within this unit?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: Not directly. But on one occasion, the International Committee of the Red Cross, sometime towards the end of 1993 and early 1994, asked to visit one of the facilities, this being the School of Music in Zenica, since they had indicia that some citizens were being detained there, citizens of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever receive reports in 1994-1995 with regard to discipline problems in the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: During the briefing sessions I mentioned in the morning, the group of us that was in Sarajevo, since the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had its forward post in Zenica as well as in Kakanj, in any case, those of us in Sarajevo did not receive any specific information on anything negative that would have to do with any activities of the 7th Muslim Brigade. By way of illustration, in 1993, when Commander Delic, in September, sent me to inspect the 2nd Corps, certain individuals in Zenica, citizens, complained of a degree of pressure exerted by that unit. In the morning, when they would carry out their physical exercise, they would run through a part of the city, yelling "Allahu Akbar." Perhaps it is unimportant or marginal, but this is what I heard about that brigade at the time, and I was told that it caused fear in the part of Zenica where they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was going to show two videotapes, so I think they're going to take longer than three minutes. If we can break now, I would request that we break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I'd like to show the witness some clips from a videotape, and it's P06028. And I believe that we don't have -- do we have the written transcription of the videotape or -- the translators, I believe, are going to be reading the transcription on their own.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We invite the commander of the 7th Corps brigade, General Mehmed Alagic, to speak."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Witness, could you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, can you identify the persons in this photograph -- this video?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: The commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Rasim Delic; and the commander of the 3rd Corps, Sakib Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see three people on the picture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't recognize the third person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us who is Mr. Rasim Delic and who is Mr. Mahmuljin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Rasim Delic is wearing a camouflage uniform; whereas, Mr. Mahmuljin has a solid hue wind jacket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the picture -- the clothes look the same to me for all three. Maybe if we can say the one on the right, the one on the left, the one in the center, something like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person in the middle is the commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. To his left and to our right is Sakib Mahmuljin, commander of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Salam Alaikum. Fellow soldiers, brothers, Mujahedin, I come to convey congratulations from the soldiers and the officers of the 7th Corps, and from your fellow soldiers. You deserve the name that has been bestowed upon you. You deserved it a long time ago and reaffirmed it, in particular, together with the soldiers of the 7th Corps under conditions incomprehensible to the mind. You jointly achieved victory and freed Vlasic. "Many brothers who have given their lives for Bosnia-Herzegovina gave it for its integrity, its unity, and all those who stand in the way of that will have to reckon with us. Therefore, dear brothers, until our final return, until our final victory, Salam Alaikum.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us who is giving that speech?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt a little bit? At the beginning of this clip, I heard the interpreter translate something and mention certain words which are not on here. Who was he greeting? We would like to know who he was greeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, do you know what this video clip is about?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: It was a commemoration, a function of one of the units. I don't know which one. He greeted the commander of the 7th Corps, Mr. Mehmed Alagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There's the 7th Corps and yet another name. If we could go back to the beginning of that clip, please, just that first sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. It's not the 7th Corps, but the commander of the 7th Corps who addressed the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we can go back to the beginning of the clip, please, I would like to hear the first sentence in the clip, the translation thereof.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We invite the commander of the 7th Corps Brigade, General Mehmed Alagic, to speak. "Salam Alaikum. Fellow soldiers, brothers, and the Mujahedin..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the transcript reflects what we can hear on the recording, that the man says that, "We invite the commander of the 7th Corps"; whereas, here we have "the 7th Corps brigade." It is not correct. Lines 5 and 6 are incorrect. Perhaps we can replay the footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we replay the footage, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We invite the 7th Corps Brigade, General Mehmed Alagic, to speak." Brigadier general. "Salam Alaikum. Fellow soldiers, brothers, and Mujahedin, I came to convey sincere congratulations from the soldiers and officers of the 7th Corps, and from your fellow soldiers."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The only word missing is "and" between "soldiers" and "Mujahedin."

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So I would like to ask the witness if he knows.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Again, can you describe what this event was, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: I don't know what this was about. It was a celebration of sorts in a unit; and, from the footage, I concluded that it is the 7th Muslim Brigade. However, before seeing it, I had no knowledge of it, of what this event was about. When the 7th Corps commander is mentioned, as I said, he addressed the 7th Muslim Brigade on their behalf. We are talking about the 7th Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Mr. Alagic. Your Honour, you also used the word "Mujahedin," but they are not "Mujahedin." They are "Mudzahirs," meaning refugees, people driven from their ancestral homes. It has nothing to do with the word "Mujahedin," nothing whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a problem with that explanation, Mr. Divjak. I thought I heard from the B/C/S expressly that you used the word "Mujahedin" and not "Mudzahir." Did you attend this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. But I do believe that he said "Mudzahir" and not "Mujahedin."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We believe the speaker said "Mujahedin."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And we can play the tape again if you want to hear that word. You see, the problem is that you are being asked to explain if you know what the occasion was, not to rewrite the script. Remember not to try and rewrite the script. For the sake of the witness, maybe that clip should be played again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Fellow soldiers, brothers, and Mujahids, I come to convey sincere congratulations from the soldiers and officers of the 7th Corps."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did you hear that, Witness? Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in our language, the word "Mujahid" and "Mujahedin" do not mean the same. "Mujahid" means "guest." A Mujahedin is a member of an Arabic unit. "Mujahid," however, is a refugee. This is very important to us, and I can stand corrected, if I am mistaken, by the witness or by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if he were to address a group of Mujahedin, he would put the accent in the wrong -- in a different place.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I object to, again, Madam Vidovic is testifying and educating -- allegedly educating Your Honours. If she wants to bring in someone to clarify different terms, that's one thing; but to stand here and to discuss this with Your Honours is another. We will have the tape enhanced, Your Honours, for another witness, and we'll replay it, and at this point move on. The word is what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any response, Madam?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what is entered in the transcript should be correct. I'm asking for the correct version to be entered, and that is "Mujahid" rather than "Mujahedin."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are telling us, Madam, what various words mean in B/C/S: "Mujahid," "Mujahedin," and "Mudzahir." Now, there are three words here, and I think you need a witness to clarify that. I think I'm going to uphold the objection. I was about to rule you out of order when your learned friend stood up. You can call a witness to come and tell us that or you can ask this witness, and we can play this tape clip until everybody -- is it possible? You said you are going to enhance it, ma'am. How long does it take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second, sir, just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure, Your Honour. We may be able to do it overnight. Certainly, we'll try to do it before this witness is excused, since he will be on the stand for at least another day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: So can we start that speech again so we can hear it from the beginning, please? From the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We invite the commander of the 7th Corps, Brigadier-General Mehmed Alagic, to speak." "Salam Alaikum. Fellow soldiers, brothers, and Mujahids, I came to convey sincere congratulations from the soldiers and officers of the 7th Corps, and from your fellow soldiers. You deserve the name that has been bestowed upon you. You deserved it a long time ago and reaffirmed it, in particular, together with the soldiers of the 7th Corps under conditions incomprehensible to the mind. You jointly achieved victory and freed Vlasic. "Many brothers who have given their lives for Bosnia and Herzegovina gave it for its integrity, for its unity. All those who stand in the way of that will have to reckon with us. Therefore, dear brothers, until our final return, until our final victory, Salam Alaikum.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now I would like to play a second clip from this video, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before we leave this clip, could we have some indication as to who General Alagic is addressing himself? It would appear that it would be members of the 7th Corps, but I believe that at some point it was suggested it was members of the 7th Muslim Brigade. Maybe the witness can help us out here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: The witness is -- I believe the witness stated that in the beginning, but if he is willing to state the answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I stated that I will speak the truth. Therefore, I believe what I said, when I made the distinction between "Mujahedin" and "Mudzahir," should be recorded. "Mudzahir" is a person or family driven from his, her, or their ancestral home. I explained that the members of this brigade, for the most part, were young men who had been expelled, for the most part, from the Drina Valley. The commander who addressed the gathering, the unit - and I now know what unit it is; however, I did not before seeing the footage - addressed the 7th Muslim unit, which on that day was renamed the Chivalrous Brigade because of the results it achieved during the defence struggle in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Alagic is commander of the 7th Corps. He conveyed congratulations on behalf of the units of the 7th Corps, and he thanked the 7th Muslim Brigade for having helped them in taking over an elevation, this being Mount Vlasic, which was of tactical and strategic importance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So can I just clarify a bit here? This would seem to imply that members of the 7th Muslim Brigade, under the 3rd Corps, would have assisted troops of the 7th Corps in freeing Mount Vlasic? Is that the correct interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question, please: This 7th Muslim Brigade, was it included in the 7th Corps? Was it part of the 7th Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was part of the 3rd Corps. However, when the units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina would undertake an attack, they would join certain formations. During the attack on Vlasic, the 7th Corps units and the 7th Muslim Brigade from the 3rd Corps took part jointly. They both achieved the victory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Any further questions from the Bench right now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for conducting the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I might as well ask my question at this point. You told us, sir, that the Mudzahir were refugees who had been expelled from their homes in the Drina Valley, and you said that they were an elite unit who were used on the front line. What qualified them to be used on the front line; the fact that they were expelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was their driving force. In the area where they were fighting, that area remained defended. They were the best equipped and armed unit. They were well trained. However, just like the other brigades, they had no heavy weaponry. They were very good at infiltrating in the rear of the aggressor to carry out sabotage strikes, thus achieving almost the same result as those units which enjoyed artillery support. They had a reputation, that unit, because wherever they appeared, they assisted greatly in successfully carrying out combat tasks. I know that during a critical period --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that. All I wanted to hear, and you've explained it, was what was the criterion or criteria for their choice as elite staff. From your earlier testimony, I was left with the impression that the only qualification was because they were refugees, but now you've explained that they were highly trained. Now, was this specialised training given only to the refugees from Drina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That unit had other men from Zenica, Bugojno, and all parts of the territory gravitating towards Zenica, but most of them were refugees from the Drina Valley, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the other people from other parts of Bosnia who didn't come from Drina were not refugees, necessarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. For example, if we are talking about the 1st Corps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no. Wait a minute. We're talking about this corps, this unit, this unit, the Mudzahir. You're saying it was composed of people from other areas like Zenica, and I'm asking you, very simply, whether other people from other areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina who didn't come from the Drina Valley, were they also refugees or not? That's what I want to know. If you say "yes" or "no," you will satisfy me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were people from other areas, not only from the Drina Valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. Can I cut you short?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But those who were refugees from Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't bother --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question simply is: Were there people from other areas, from Zenica and other areas, who formed part of the Mudzahir, were they also refugees? Just say "yes" or "no," sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So this whole unit was composed of refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Not all of it. Part of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I just asked you whether other people from other regions were refugees, and you said, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and I maintain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then if the people from Drina Valley were refugees and people from other areas were also refugees, then the entire area was refugees, was composed of refugees. It must follow logically.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is not what I said. I said that in that unit, there were refugees from Banja Luka as well, and that there were also soldiers, citizens in that unit hailing from the environs of Zenica. In that brigade there were also Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And my question to you simply was: These people from the environs of Zenica, were they refugees like the people from Banja Luka and the Drina Valley? And what is your answer to that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat what I've already said. There were also refugees from other parts of the country as well. That part around Zenica, which was controlled by the Croatian Defence Council, they had been expelled, and some of them made their way to that brigade. I don't know what the percentage was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I'll ask you the very question I asked you right in the beginning: Was this Mudzahir unit composed entirely of refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's another question I'd like to put to you, Witness, a question related once again to the composition of the 7th Muslim Brigade: Was there another criterion? I'm talking about the composition of the brigade. Were all these people Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They are representatives of both the Serbian and the Croatian peoples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, the only criterion for membership of this brigade was that these people were refugees, they had been expelled from their homes, from the regions they hailed from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the exact percentage, but I do believe that two-thirds of the unit were refugees. I don't know the exact figures, but I do believe that two-thirds of the unit were people who had been expelled from the Drina River Valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're telling us, therefore, that in that unit, there were people who were not refugees. Let's talk about these people. What was the criterion that prevailed, that made them members of this brigade? Why did they become members of this brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They could have just simply been mobilised into that unit; namely, the Municipal Defence Secretariat, the Secretariat for the Defence of Zenica, could have assigned to that unit also others who were free to join the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Sartorio.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. President asked you a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: And I'd like to go up to the transcript, if I may, to Judge Moloto's last comment. It's just above the screen. Well, I believe it is page 44, line 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It says: "Was this Mudzahir unit composed entirely of refugees?" Can you tell us what a Mudzahir unit is?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: That Mudzahir unit, the 7th Muslims unit, was composed mostly of people that had been expelled from the Drina River Valley, from where entire families had been expelled. It was composed of members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the general area of Zenica. And as I have said, the Secretariat for National Defence could also assign to that unit others as well; namely, people who were not refugees. So I repeat -- and I also repeat that there had been members of other peoples in that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Sir, do you know what position General Alagic held before the current position in the videotape?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: To my recollection, he was the commander of the 7th Operations Group.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Now before we go back to the videotape, were you aware of this event prior to viewing the videotape?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: You never heard about this ceremony as deputy commander of the army?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: I'd like to play the next clip, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We invite the Emir of the 7th Muslim Chivalrous Mountain Brigade, Mahmut Efendija Karalic, to greet the assembled. "In the name of Allah," this was in Arabic, "fellow soldiers, dear guests, and friends -- fellow soldiers, dear guests and friends, Salam Alaikum." Peace be with you. The crowd replies: Peace be with you. "Alaikum Salam." Efendija Karalic: "After all these wonderful words, so many of them, I am at a loss for words. I would like to quote and translate. I quoted a saying from the Qu'ran that I quoted for the first time when the president of the Presidency visited you, but I didn't translate it then, so I will do so today. "The glorious Allah, glory be unto him, says that: 'Perform your duties, and your deeds will be seen by Allah Almighty, his prophet and righteous people.' "This has been confirmed here today. We have been working for over two years, and we are performing one of the most honourable tasks. We are defending our native land. We are defending our faith, our honour, and our dignity. We are defending the innocent. We are defending innocent lives that are endangered simply because they say that Allah is their master and simply because they are Muslims who live in these parts. "That is why it is an honour, especially because it is being bestowed on us this day, the third day of Kurban Bajram, and because the commander of the General Staff, Army General Rasim Delic, is personally present, and because this honour bears the signature of our honorary commander, the president of the Presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. "In the name of that, I congratulate all of you on this important honour, but with a word of caution. The honour is flattering and comes at a much-needed time, but any honour only carries with it more responsibility for us to continue, with Allah's help, to continue as long as our national and military leadership demands it of us, and for as long as there is even one Muslim life that is endangered in these parts. "I hope that with Allah's help, we will live up to this honour and that there will be more awards in this world. But what we hope for the most and what we are fighting for is that Ishala," with God's help, "we will receive the greatest reward from the master of the universe, Allah. Glory be unto him."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we get the number of this clip, ma'am? The first one was P06028.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: It's all the same videotape, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Yes. And there is one more speech by General Delic, and then we will ask that this be put in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I was unsure about the identity of the gentleman who spoke on the second clip here.

utterances.speaker: MS. SARTORIO
utterances.text: Do you know who was this last -- this speaker just now?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN DIVJAK
utterances.text: I don't know the man and I didn't attend that, but it can be seen from the announcement who that was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
